ops.collect-status
Charm observes CollectStatusEvent for app/unit status aggregation.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
observe-event events: CollectAppStatusEvent, CollectUnitStatusEvent, CollectStatusEvent
import module: charmed_kubeflow_chisme.components
import module: ops_sunbeam
import module: coordinated_workers
import module: single_kernel_mongo
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Available since
ops 2.5
Notes

Library-mediated status handling is detected as positive evidence (CALIBRATION #10, extended #11, extended #15):

- `charmed_kubeflow_chisme.components` charms manage status through the `CharmReconciler`/component framework, not via direct `unit.status = ...` assignment or an explicit collect-status observer.

- `ops_sunbeam` (any sub-module) charms inherit a base operator class that aggregates status across handlers.

- `coordinated_workers` (Observability CCA framework — tempo, parca, mimir, loki) — `Coordinator`/`Worker` base classes handle status as part of the reconcile cycle.

- `single_kernel_mongo` (mongodb-operator + mongodb-k8s-operator shim) — charm.py delegates to `AbstractMongoCharm`; status handling lives in the upstream library. Surfaced by the 2026-06-13 30-charm collect-status audit. In all cases the charm is using status idiomatically for its framework; flagging clear-gap on "has integrations" would be wrong.

ops.relation-app-data
Charm reads/writes application-scope relation data.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
regex pattern: relation\.data\[\s*(self\.app|event\.app|self\.model\.app|relation\.app|event\.relation\.app)\s*\]
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Regex because the subscript form is hard to express as a call pattern. Covers both writer-side reads (`self.app`/`event.app`) and remote-side reads (`relation.app`, the canonical form when a requirer reads provider app data). 2026-05-26 spike found `relation.app` is the most-common form across the corpus slice — without it the detector under-counted significantly. Still misses aliased references (`app = self.app; relation.data[app]`); acceptable for v1.

ops.pebble-ready
Charm observes PebbleReadyEvent.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
observe-event events: PebbleReadyEvent
regex pattern: \bon\.[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*_pebble_ready\b
regex pattern: \bon\[\s*[^\]]+\s*\]\.pebble_ready\b
regex pattern: getattr\s*\(\s*[^,)]+\.on\s*,\s*['"][a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*_pebble_ready['"]
regex pattern: self\.on\.events\(\)
import module: charmed_kubeflow_chisme.components
import module: ops_sunbeam
import module: coordinated_workers
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Four real-world forms:

- `observe(self.on.<container>_pebble_ready, ...)` (attribute)

- `observe(self.on['<container>'].pebble_ready, ...)` (literal subscript)

- `observe(self.on[var].pebble_ready, ...)` (variable subscript — used when the container name is computed at __init__ time, e.g. airbyte)

- `observe(getattr(self.on, "<container>_pebble_ready"), ...)` (getattr form, used by some monorepo frameworks, e.g. kafka-k8s) The event is always per-container — the class-name detector almost never fires. Regex matches the `on.X` token alone (not the surrounding `observe(...)`) because the call arguments can span multiple lines and contain comments with stray parens, which a non-balancing regex can't traverse safely.

Library-mediated handling is detected as positive evidence:

- `charmed_kubeflow_chisme.components` (Kubeflow chisme provides a `PebbleServiceComponent` that subscribes to pebble-ready internally)

- `ops_sunbeam` (any sub-module — Sunbeam base classes `WSGIPebbleHandler`/`ServicePebbleHandler` and their OVN variants `ops_sunbeam.ovn.container_handlers.*` all wire up pebble-ready internally; widened from a single sub-path per CALIBRATION #7) The reconcile-all idiom `for ev in self.on.events().values(): self.framework.observe(ev, ...)` (mysql-router-{k8s,}-operator) also subscribes to pebble-ready without ever naming the event, so we accept `self.on.events()` as evidence of presence (CALIBRATION #8).

A charm using any of these patterns is handling pebble-ready properly, even if no direct `observe(... pebble_ready ...)` call appears in src/.

pebble.checks
Charm defines pebble layer checks.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: ops.pebble; names: CheckDict, Check
yaml-key files: **/*.yaml, **/*.yml; key: checks
regex pattern: (?<![a-zA-Z_])["']?checks["']?\s*:\s*(?:[{\[]|$)
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Pebble layers are built inline as Python dicts (`"checks": {...}`) at least as often as in yaml files, so the regex matches both: quoted or unquoted `checks:` followed by `{`, `[`, or end-of-line. The negative lookbehind avoids matching `health_checks:` and similar suffixes.

pebble.log-forwarding
Charm forwards workload logs via pebble log targets.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: ops.pebble; names: LogTarget, LogTargetDict
import module: charms.loki_k8s; names: LogForwarder
regex pattern: \blog[-_]targets["']?\s*[:\]]
yaml-key key: log-targets
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Log targets live under a mapping key inside a pebble layer, and charms write that layer as a Python dict — so the key carries its own closing quote (`"log-targets": {...}`), or is reached by subscript (`layer["log-targets"] = {}`). The original `\blog[-_]targets\s*:` pattern matched neither, only the bare YAML form. Hence the optional quote and the `[:\]]` tail. The `yaml-key` arm covers layers kept in standalone *.yaml files, which `_select_files` (Python-only) never hands the regex.

`LogForwarder` (loki_push_api) is the idiomatic route: the lib injects log-targets into the layer on the charm's behalf, so a charm using it is forwarding logs without ever naming the key itself. Charms importing `ops.pebble.LogTarget`/`LogTargetDict` for typing count too, though most build the layer from plain dicts.

pebble.restart-delay
Charm tunes pebble service restart/backoff timing.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
regex pattern: \b(restart[-_]delay|backoff[-_](delay|factor|limit))["']?\s*[:\]]
yaml-key keys: backoff-delay, backoff-factor, backoff-limit
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Same quoting problem as pebble.log-forwarding: the keys appear as Python dict keys in a layer literal (`"backoff-delay": "24h"`), so the closing quote has to be optional. `backoff-limit` completes the trio of pebble's backoff keys; `restart-delay` isn't a pebble key but is kept for charms that spell their own config option that way.

Unit tests use ops.testing (Scenario or Harness — either form).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: scenario

Looks in
Python files under the charm's tests/ (or the monorepo's shared tests/integration/ when it has none) (scope tests). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Aggregate "has ops.testing unit tests" signal — kept for backwards compatibility with v1 dashboards. The two sub-features below (`.harness` and `.scenario`) split this into the migration-relevant forms; prefer those for actionable scoring. ops-scenario.context-identity
Unit tests name the app or unit under test via Context(app_name=/unit_id=).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
call-kwarg attr: Context; keyword: app_name
call-kwarg attr: Context; keyword: unit_id
Looks in
Python files under the charm's tests/ (or the monorepo's shared tests/integration/ when it has none) (scope tests). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

`testing.Context` grew `app_name` and `unit_id` so a test can pin the identity the charm sees. Without them the Context invents one, which is fine until the charm's own behaviour depends on its name or unit number — leader-only paths keyed off unit 0, resources named after the app, log lines asserted on.

Matched on the keyword being present rather than on its value: the value is whatever the test wants to call itself, and any of them is the same adoption fact. `attr: Context` catches both the bare `Context(...)` and the `testing.Context(...)` module-import form, which the `.scenario` row above shows is the common spelling.

A flat percentage over the corpus mostly measures how old everyone's `ops` pin is, since these arguments are recent, so read the row's by-ops-pin cells rather than its corpus total (#74). Those cells bucket on `ops`, and this is an `ops-scenario` API, so they are a proxy here rather than the gate itself — the two move together in practice, since a charm bumps its test pin when it bumps `ops`.

testing.pytest-operator
Integration tests use pytest-operator (python-libjuju).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: pytest_operator
regex pattern: def\s+test_\w*\s*\([^)]*\bops_test\b
Looks in
Python files under the charm's tests/ (or the monorepo's shared tests/integration/ when it has none) (scope tests). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The predecessor to jubilant, and the other half of the adoption dashboard's integration-testing split (jubilant / pytest-operator / neither). Two arms because the plugin is usually reached through its `ops_test` fixture rather than an import: a test module that only takes `ops_test` as a parameter never names `pytest_operator`. A charm can legitimately hit both arms, and a charm mid-migration can hit this *and* `jubilant.integration-tests` — the dashboard counts jubilant first so a part-migrated charm reads as adopted.

testing.zaza
Integration tests are driven by zaza (tests/tests.yaml bundles).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
zaza-config
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The third harness in the adoption dashboard's integration-testing split, alongside jubilant and pytest-operator. Zaza is the OpenStack charms' framework: the suite is `tests/tests.yaml` naming bundles and `zaza.*` test classes rather than a `tests/integration/` directory of pytest modules, so neither Python-file detector can see it and these charms read as having no integration tests at all without this one. The detector follows the charm's `tests/` up to the repo root, which is where `sunbeam-charms` keeps its `tests/<suite>/tests.yaml` set for all 80-odd charms beneath. Descriptive-only; absent → not-applicable.

testing.juju-2
CI installs a Juju 2.x (in practice 2.9) to test against.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
ci-juju-channel major: 2; follow_uses: True
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Read by evaluating the repo's CI (`charmtally/ci_juju.py`) rather than by matching text: inputs are bound over their defaults, strategy matrices expanded and reusable workflows followed, so a channel a shared workflow merely *defaults* to — `operator-workflows`' `integration_test.yaml` defaults to 2.9/stable, and almost every caller overrides it — counts only where nobody overrides it. Pass or fail does not matter (`continue-on-error` is ignored): the question is what CI runs against. An install whose channel is `vars.*` or otherwise unknowable, or that names no channel at all, counts towards no version. Repo-level, like `testing.concierge`: every sub-charm of a monorepo reads its repo's answer. Descriptive-only; absent → not-applicable.

CI installs a Juju 4.x to test against — any minor, or the bare 4 track.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
ci-juju-channel major: 4; follow_uses: True
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

Read by evaluating the repo's CI (`charmtally/ci_juju.py`) rather than by matching text: inputs are bound over their defaults, strategy matrices expanded and reusable workflows followed, so a channel a shared workflow merely *defaults* to — `operator-workflows`' `integration_test.yaml` defaults to 2.9/stable, and almost every caller overrides it — counts only where nobody overrides it. Pass or fail does not matter (`continue-on-error` is ignored): the question is what CI runs against. An install whose channel is `vars.*` or otherwise unknowable, or that names no channel at all, counts towards no version. Repo-level, like `testing.concierge`: every sub-charm of a monorepo reads its repo's answer. Descriptive-only; absent → not-applicable.

testing.pytest-jubilant
Integration tests use the pytest-jubilant plugin.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: pytest_jubilant
regex pattern: def\s+test_\w*\s*\([^)]*\bjuju(?:_factory)?\b
Looks in
Python files under the charm's tests/ (or the monorepo's shared tests/integration/ when it has none) (scope tests). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The plugin half of jubilant: `jubilant.integration-tests` sees the library, this sees the pytest plugin that hands out a temporary model. Two arms for the same reason `testing.pytest-operator` has two — the plugin is normally reached through its `juju` / `juju_factory` fixture rather than an import, and a test module that only takes the fixture never names `pytest_jubilant`. Deliberately a row of its own rather than a third arm of the integration-testing split: a charm using the plugin is using jubilant too, so both are expected to fire together and neither has to arbitrate the other away. The fixture arm is the looser of the two — a charm that writes its own `juju` fixture in `conftest.py` matches it as well — which is acceptable here, because such a fixture is still handing a `jubilant.Juju` to the test.

testing.concierge
The repo's CI provisions its test environment with Concierge.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
repo-file files: .github/workflows/*.yaml, .github/workflows/*.yml; pattern: \bconcierge\s+(prepare|restore|status)\b; follow_uses: True
repo-file files: .github/workflows/*.yaml, .github/workflows/*.yml; pattern: snap\s+install[^\n]*\bconcierge\b|CONCIERGE_[A-Z0-9_]+; follow_uses: True
repo-file files: concierge.yaml, concierge.yml, concierge-*.yaml, concierge-*.yml
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The first `repo-file` detectors in the catalogue, and the reason the kind exists: `_select_files` returns `*.py` only, and every other file-independent detector globs from the *charm* root, so a monorepo sub-charm can never see `.github/` — which is where the answer to this question lives, for every charm in the repo.

Three detectors because the shape varies and none of them dominates. A sample of 156 `canonical/*` workflow hits (2026-09-15) shows the command form is the common one — `sudo concierge prepare --trace`, usually a step or two after `sudo snap install concierge --classic` — so the command and the install are matched separately: a workflow that installs the snap and drives it from a script still counts. `CONCIERGE_*` catches the env-var configuration form (`CONCIERGE_JUJU_CHANNEL`, mongodb-k8s-operator). There is no `canonical/setup-concierge` action to match: the request named one, but it has no repository and a code search for it returns a single hit across GitHub, that one a transcript rather than a workflow.

The third detector is the committed config — repo root only. Concierge reads `concierge.yaml` from the working directory, so a root file is what a CI step invoking it bare picks up; a deeper one (`charm/concierge.yaml`) belongs to whatever runs in that directory and would be attributed to every sibling sub-charm if it were globbed for, which is a worse error than missing it.

`follow_uses: true` on the first two detectors, because a charm whose CI delegates to a reusable workflow in *another* repo shows nothing in its own `.github/`. Sized 2026-09-15 against the 460 corpus repos that are on GitHub at all (the other 111 are Launchpad or opendev and have no Actions): 61 repos / 85 charms match directly, and another 46 repos / 53 charms call a workflow that provisions with Concierge — so reading only the checkout got about 62% of the charms it should, low by a third rather than by a rounding error.

The gap was concentrated rather than spread: seven workflow files account for all 53 charms, six of them in `canonical/observability` (`_charm-quality-checks.yaml`, `_charm-release.yaml`, `charm-pull-request.yaml`, `charm-release.yaml`, `rock-pull-request.yaml`, `rock-release-dev.yaml`) and the seventh `canonical/workflows-team`'s `terraform.yaml`, which is how the four temporal charms get there. It is one team's estate, which is also why closing it moves a single library's adoption rather than the ecosystem's. The two largest reusable-workflow libraries, `canonical/data-platform-workflows` (46 files) and `canonical/operator-workflows` (22), do not use Concierge at all, so the gap never grew with them.

Resolution is transitive — two of the seven are only reached at a second hop — and only happens on a run that installed a workflow cache, so an offline scan reads what it did before rather than silently reporting fewer charms. What is left is the residual the sizing could not account for either way: 65 of the 460 repos have no `.github/` at all, and 24 of the rest call a workflow that could not be read, private or since renamed.

Attribution: a monorepo's one workflow reads as present for every sub-charm it covers, so this counts repos once per charm rather than once. That is the honest per-charm answer — all five sub-charms really are tested under Concierge — but it is not a count of *decisions*; anything wanting that should group by `repo_url`.

charmlibs.namespace
Charm imports a library from the `charmlibs` namespace package.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: charmlibs
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The PyPI `charmlibs` namespace (`charmlibs-pathops`, `charmlibs-apt`, `charmlibs-interfaces-*`) — charm-tech's replacement for Charmhub libraries vendored under `lib/charms/`. Distinct from the other `charmlibs.*` features here, which pre-date the namespace and match those vendored libs by import path (`charms.data_platform_libs`, ...). Scope is `any`: pathops in particular shows up in tests as often as in src. The per-charm *counts* behind the adoption dashboard's charmlibs share come from `__meta__.charmlibs_names`, not from this feature — a feature is a boolean, and the share needs a numerator.

charmlibs.cos-agent
Charm integrates with the grafana-agent / COS agent (consumer side).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: charms.grafana_agent; names: COSAgentProvider
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The lib defines `COSAgentProvider` (consumer side — machine charms that expose metrics to grafana-agent) and `COSAgentRequirer` (provider side — grafana-agent itself receives via Requirer). The 2026-05-26 spike showed that matching any `charms.grafana_agent` import produced a semantic false positive on `grafana-agent-operator` itself, which imports `COSAgentRequirer` because it is the target of integration. Pinning the import name to `COSAgentProvider` restricts detection to the consumer side, which is the intended "this charm integrates with COS" signal. Post-processing should additionally exclude charms whose repo provides the lib (i.e. has `lib/charms/grafana_agent/`) — belt and braces.

charmlibs.tls-certificates
Charm imports the vendored tls_certificates_interface library (pre-charmlibs).
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: charms.tls_certificates_interface
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The "before" half of the migration pair charmtally#95 asked for: the Charmhub-vendored lib (`lib/charms/tls_certificates_interface/v#/tls_certificates.py`; the module-prefix match covers every vendored version, v0-v4, without listing them). `charmlibs.interfaces.tls-certificates` below is the "after" — PyPI `charmlibs-interfaces-tls-certificates`, v1.

`charmlibs.namespace` (above) matches any import from the `charmlibs` namespace and can't say whether a given charm is on pathops, apt, or one of the interface libraries. This feature and the `charmlibs.interfaces.*` ones below narrow that down for the interfaces half, one library at a time — the only way to get a per-library adoption number rather than one lumped total, at the cost of one `features.yaml` entry per library (charmtally#95's own open question, decided in favour of the finer split).

Checked against `canonical/charmlibs`'s `interfaces/index.json` (2026-09-09): of 68 entries, 9 name a `charmlibs.interfaces.*` library in their `lib` field — auth_proxy, forward_auth, istio_metadata, k8s_backup_target, ldap, oauth, openfga, tls_certificates and tracing. (The issue that asked for this counted 8 — tracing isn't in its list — so either it shipped between the issue being filed and this check, or the issue's count missed it; either way, 9 is what's actually in the file now.) The other 59 point back at a vendored `charms.*` lib, at `cosl`, or at nothing, and get no detector: there's nothing to migrate to, and scoring them as a gap would be wrong. tls-certificates has by far the largest vendored population of the 9, which is why charmtally#95 called it out by name and why it alone gets an old-side pair here — the other 8 don't have a confirmed vendored `charms.*` predecessor to detect against (see `charmlibs.interfaces.auth-proxy`'s notes).

ops.typed-relation
Charm uses ops Relation.load / Relation.save typed-relation API.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
regex pattern: \b\w*[Rr]elation\w*\.load\s*\(\s*[A-Z]\w+
regex pattern: \b\w*[Rr]elation\w*\.save\s*\(
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The API is `Relation.load(cls, src)` / `Relation.save(obj, dst)` — the data class comes FIRST on load, and on save the first argument is an instance. The original `\.(load|save)\(relation, ModelClass\)` pattern had the argument order backwards, so it could never match a real call; its only corpus hit was a charm-lib helper (`KratosInfoData.load(self.model, ...)`).

Both arms require the receiver to be relation-ish (`relation.load(...)`, `event.relation.save(...)`, `self._peer_relation.load(...)`), which is what rules out `SomeDataClass.load(...)` helpers on other libraries. The save arm can't also check its arguments the way load does: the object being saved is written both as a variable and as a constructor call (`relation.save(TracingRequirerData(...), self.app)`), so the receiver carries the precision on its own.

ops.typed-config
Charm uses ops load_config / load_params typed-data API.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
regex pattern: \bload_config\s*\(\s*[A-Z]\w+
regex pattern: \bload_params\s*\(\s*[A-Z]\w+
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The config half of the same typed-data story as `ops.typed-relation`: `self.load_config(MyConfig)` on the charm, and `event.load_params(MyParams)` on an action event. Both take the data class as their first argument, so — as with `Relation.load` — requiring a capitalised first argument is what separates a real call from a same-named helper that takes a path or a dict.

Deliberately one feature covering both calls: a charm that types its config but not its action parameters has still adopted the API, and the adoption scorecard asks the OR of the two anyway. The action half is also counted on its own as `ops.typed-config.params`, for the feature view, which wants the two apart; this row stays the OR, so the scorecard reads the same number it always has.

how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
regex pattern: \bload_params\s*\(\s*[A-Z]\w+
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

The action arm of `ops.typed-config`, broken out because typed config and typed action parameters are separate questions to anyone reading the feature view, and the parent row — deliberately the OR of the two — cannot answer either alone.

Same detector as the parent's second arm, capitalised first argument and all, so a charm cannot be present here and absent there.

Reading the pair: this row is typed *actions*; typed *config* is the parent minus the charms that appear here and call no `load_config`. That remainder is empty across the corpus today, which is why there is no third row for it — a charm that types its action parameters and leaves its config untyped would be the first.

`expected_rare: true` because the parent is a young API with a handful of adopters, and the action half is the smaller part of that handful.

ops.tracing
Charm depends on ops[tracing] / ops-tracing.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
requirement name: ops; extra: tracing
requirement name: ops-tracing
Looks in
every Python file in the charm, excluding vendored charm libraries (scope any). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Available since
ops 2.21
Notes

A dependency fact rather than a code one: `ops-tracing` is the package that ships the OpenTelemetry exporter and the `tracing` relation plumbing, and a charm that has not added it cannot emit a span whatever its source says. `ops[tracing]` and a bare `ops-tracing` pin are the same dependency spelled two ways, so both arms are counted.

This says the charm has *turned tracing on*, not that it uses it: a charm that adds the dependency and never instruments anything beyond what ops emits itself still reads as present here. Manual instrumentation is a separate signal.

The blind spot is a charm that pins its dependencies somewhere the scan does not read — a lock file, a constraints file, or a base image. Those read as absent rather than being guessed at.

ops.tracing.manual
Charm instruments its own code rather than only what ops traces for it.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
import module: opentelemetry
call attr: start_as_current_span
call attr: tracing.set_destination
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Available since
ops 2.21
Notes

The other half of `ops.tracing`: that one says the charm has turned tracing on, this one says someone went further than the dependency. `ops[tracing]` already emits a span per hook and per Juju call, so the charm-level picture costs nothing; a span around a workload call or a long-running loop has to be written by hand, and that is what this row counts.

Only meaningful against charms that have tracing enabled at all — `ops.tracing` is the denominator, and a charm without the dependency scores `not-applicable` here rather than as a gap.

Three signals, `src` only:

* an `opentelemetry` import anywhere in `src`, which is how a charm gets a tracer in the first place;

* a `start_as_current_span` call, the usual span-per-block idiom, matched as a call suffix so the decorator and context-manager forms both count;

* `ops.tracing.set_destination`, which is a charm choosing where its traces go instead of leaving that to the `tracing` relation.

Two blind spots. `from ops.tracing import set_destination` followed by a bare `set_destination(...)` is invisible, because a one-segment suffix here would also match any charm helper of that name — the dotted form is the safer half of the trade. And instrumentation that lives in a vendored library rather than in `src` reads as absent, which is the same treatment every other `src`-scoped feature gives library-mediated code.

ops.typed-config.handled-errors
Charm handles typed config/param validation failure instead of erroring.
how it’s detected
Present when any of these match
call-kwarg attr: load_config; keyword: errors; equals: blocked
call-kwarg attr: load_params; keyword: errors; equals: fail
Looks in
Python files under the charm's src/ and lib/, excluding tests and vendored charm libraries (scope src). Detectors that read metadata, YAML or the repository’s CI read those files whatever the scope.
Notes

A sub-row of `ops.typed-config`: that one says the charm calls the typed-data API, this one says it handles the call failing.

`load_config(C, errors='blocked')` catches the validation failure, sets a BlockedStatus the operator can read, and exits successfully. The default, `errors='raise'`, leaves the exception to reach the hook boundary, so the unit goes to `error` and Juju holds every subsequent hook — including the `config-changed` that would fix it — until someone runs `juju resolved`. That is the same user-visible failure the hand-rolled parsing typed config replaced. `load_params` spells its half `errors='fail'`, which fails the action rather than the unit; both are counted here for the same reason `ops.typed-config` counts both calls.

Two known blind spots, both deliberate:

* A charm that takes the default and wraps the call in its own `try`/`except` setting a status is doing the right thing by other means, and reads here as absent.

* `errors=` passed as a variable or splatted in from a dict is not visible to a scan, and is likewise counted as absent rather than guessed at either way.
